For this hackathon, I would like to score very very high up on the leaderboard for entire. How do I do that?



<pasted_content id="686a">
Entire at Agentic AI Hack Zürich 2026
Entire team on site

J
Joseph Katsioloudes
Developer Relations
01
What is Entire?
Entire is the git forge for AI-native teams. The Entire CLI captures every AI coding agent session, so the reasoning behind the code stays with the git repo, right next to your code. Then, Continuous Memory (Entire Graph + Entire Brain) turns those sessions into living knowledge for your agents. Your repo learns from every attempt, every fix, every decision, and your agents get smarter because of it.

Learn more from our docs 

02
Features you can build with
Checkpoints
Connect a Git commit to the agent sessions and decisions behind it.

Agentic Search
You or your agent can search semantically through previous commits, sessions, and decisions, or literal source text, across pushed, indexed repositories.

Entire Graph
Hands your agent a map of your codebase and can save up to 71% in token spend. Analyzes local code to find implementations, trace relationships, and investigate potential change impact.

Entire Brain
The memory layer that lives in your repo, not in one agent. Start a session in Claude Code, pick it up in Codex, and the context carries over.

Agent integrations
Capture work from supported coding agents, or add another through the Agent Integration Protocol.

03
Ideas to build
01
Hand off work between agents without losing context
Start a feature in Claude Code and finish it in Codex. Use Brain to carry the decisions and rejected approaches across, and Graph to point both agents at the same code. Show the second agent picking up the work without being re-briefed.

02
Prove what Continuous Memory saves
Run the same set of tasks with and without Graph and Brain. Compare tokens, time and correctness, using entire graph stats for the token savings, and publish the results with links to the sessions behind each run.

03
A debugger for agent mistakes
Start with a failing test or bug, inspect the affected code with Graph, and trace relevant checkpoints to find where an incorrect assumption entered the implementation. Show the evidence behind the diagnosis.

04
A reviewer that checks intent
Compare the original request with the committed change. Flag missed requirements, unexpected behavior, and claims that lack test evidence, with links to the relevant transcript and code.

05
A "before you build" assistant
Search previous sessions for similar attempts and rejected approaches, then use Graph to locate reusable code. Produce a short briefing before the agent starts editing.

06
An architecture drift detector
Compare Graph snapshots across commits to spot new dependencies or unexpected coupling. Attach checkpoint context explaining why each change was introduced.

07
An onboarding guide you can question
Let a new teammate ask, "How does authentication work, and why was it designed this way?" Combine current code relationships with historical decisions and source links.

08
A regression test scout
Use a checkpoint's changes and Graph relationships to suggest behaviors that need tests. Consult session context for edge cases the agent discussed but may not have covered.

09
A checkpoint-to-demo generator
Turn a checkpoint into a concise walkthrough: the problem, key decisions, implementation, and recorded validation. Generate a shareable page with links back to the evidence.

10
An integration for your favorite unsupported agent
Build an adapter that captures its sessions and connects them to commits. Ship it with lifecycle tests and a working checkpoint demo.

Other
Feel free to be creative and impress!

04
Connect your repository
Sign in
Everyone on the team signs in to Entire with Sign in with GitHub and authorizes the Entire GitHub App when prompted. You can do this at any time, before or after the next step.

GitHub organization admin: import the repository
A GitHub organization admin installs the Entire GitHub App on the organization by following the onboarding. Nothing repository-related appears for anyone in the team until this step is done.

Sign-in order doesn't matter, but the repository and its sessions only show up after the admin has configured access.

Once the admin has imported the repository, it appears for the whole team. No invites and no permission setup: access follows the GitHub collaborator list, so everyone keeps the same roles they have on GitHub.

Changes can take up to an hour to sync. If the repository is missing from your list, ask your organization admin.
Next: install the CLI and start your first checkpoint (following section).

05
Push your first agent session
Install Entire, then enable it from your repository
Shell

Copy
# macOS/Linux:
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash

# Windows:
irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 | iex

cd your-repo
entire enable
Work as normal by starting a new agent session, ask your agent to make a focused change, and review the result.

Commit the change
Shell

Copy
git add path/to/changed-file
git commit -m "Build my first feature with Entire"
Choose yes if prompted to link the commit to session context.

Inspect your checkpoint
Shell

Copy
entire checkpoint list
entire checkpoint explain HEAD
A normal committed checkpoint needs both captured agent context and a Git commit. Full walkthrough 

06
Turn on Trails
This is how Entire reimagines Code Review in the AI era. You'll see Trails in action during our demo. To use it in your own repository:

Request access from an Entiron after you onboard on Entire
Trails is behind a feature flag. Once you've signed up, fill in the Trails access form and someone from the Entire team will enable Trails for you.

Enable Trails in your repository
Open your repository in Entire, go to Settings → General, and turn on Runners, Auto build on push, and Trails. This requires admin permission on the repository.

Each Trail is currently backed by a GitHub PR for CI.
Add the default Runners
Runners evaluate each Trail and publish findings. From the repository root, run:

Shell

Copy
entire runner setup -y
Then commit and push the generated .entire/ files.

You or your agent: create a Trail and work normally
Your coding agent already knows how to use Trails through the CLI, so just ask it to create one. Or run:

Shell

Copy
entire trail create
Commit and push to the Trail branch as usual. The Trail updates automatically, Runners evaluate each push, and your team can review and merge from the Trail.

07
Continuous Memory
Optional
Optional: only if you are building with Entire Graph/Brain.

A
Install and activate entire-graph
You or your agents can install the entire-graph plugin. Activate it once per repository:

Shell

Copy
entire plugin install graph
entire graph init-agents --repo .
The second command creates .entire/graph-agent.md with the agent instructions, and adds a short block to your AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md telling your agents to use entire-graph.

Commit those three files so it applies to your whole team, then start a fresh agent session. You'll know it worked when your agent's first move is entire-graph search instead of a grep.

Start using entire-graph
Restart the agent so it picks up the new instructions, then ask in plain language: Where is request routing implemented? The agent runs graph queries, reads the code the graph points to, and answers with citations.

To see what it saved you, run:

Shell

Copy
entire graph stats --repo .
It reads your Claude Code session transcripts, counts how many times your agent used the graph instead of grepping and reading files, and estimates the tokens it saved. For how entire-graph works, installation, and troubleshooting, see the Graph docs .

B
Install entire-brain
Make sure the Entire CLI and entire-graph are installed first (steps above).

Without entire-graph, setup reports the semantic index as unavailable; sessions, docs and facts still work. Without the Entire CLI there are no sessions to read, and entire-brain falls back to code, docs and Git history.
Shell

Copy
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash
The script downloads a prebuilt binary, checks it against the release checksums, and registers it with the CLI as the entire-brain plugin.

Or build from source
Activate your agent
From your project repository, install the agent instructions:

Shell

Copy
entire brain init-agents
This embeds your existing sessions (if any) and creates or updates the agent instructions at .entire/agent-guide.md. Rerunning the command replaces this file. It also updates AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md with references to the guide inside managed blocks; your text outside those blocks is preserved.

Review the generated files and commit them together when the instructions should apply to your team. When entire-graph is installed, the guide tells agents to use entire-brain for prior decisions and entire-graph to locate and inspect code. Restart your agent or reload its repository instructions so it picks up the guide.

Using an MCP client?
Print this repository's configuration:

Shell

Copy
entire brain mcp --print-config
Then register it with an MCP-capable client. For example, in Claude Code:

Shell

Copy
claude mcp add entire-brain -- entire brain mcp
See the agent integration guide and coordination contract for more setup details.

08
Let your agent help
Your coding agent can fix setup problems and look up the Entire docs for you, so you don't have to leave the terminal.

Something not working? Ask your agent to run doctor
If a session doesn't show up or checkpoints look wrong, ask your agent to run entire doctor. It checks the repository for stuck sessions, hook config drift and disconnected checkpoint branches, then reports each issue and how to fix it.

Shell

Copy
entire doctor
Add --force to fix every issue without prompting. What doctor checks 

Give your agent the Entire docs
The docs are served as an MCP server, so your agent can search them and answer questions about Entire while you build. For example, in Claude Code:

Shell

Copy
claude mcp add --transport http entire-docs https://docs.entire.io/mcp
Not using MCP? Point your agent at docs.entire.io/llms.txt, an index of every docs page in Markdown.
</pasted_content id="686a">


Can you come up with a plan please?

The pasted brief doesn't say how the leaderboard is scored, so this plan is built on assumptions. I'd ask the Entire team on site (Joseph or anyone else) what's scored. If it's checkpoints or sessions pushed, usage depth counts. If it's judged on projects, the idea and demo count. The plan below covers both.

## Plan

**Phase 0: Setup (first 30–45 min, done before anything else)**
1. One teammate signs in with GitHub. A GitHub org admin installs the Entire GitHub App and imports the repo. Sync can take up to an hour, so start now. If `planworldsimulator` is under your personal account, check whether a personal repo is supported or move it to an org.
2. Run `entire enable` in the repo and make a first small commit linked to a checkpoint. Confirm it with `entire checkpoint list` and `entire doctor`.
3. Ask for Trails access via the form, since it's behind a feature flag. Then turn on Runners, Auto build on push and Trails in the repo settings, and run `entire runner setup -y`.
4. Install Graph and Brain:
   - `entire plugin install graph`
   - `entire graph init-agents --repo .`
   - the Brain install script
   - `entire brain init-agents`
   - Commit the generated `.entire/`, `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` changes.
5. Add the docs MCP: `claude mcp add --transport http entire-docs https://docs.entire.io/mcp`.

**Phase 1: Maximize visible usage**
- Do all work through Entire-captured agent sessions. Make small, frequent commits, each linked to a checkpoint.
- Work on Trails, with each Trail backed by a PR, so Runners evaluate every push.
- Use Graph and Brain in every session, so `entire graph stats` shows real token savings.
- Use a second agent (Codex) for part of the work, so Brain's cross-agent handoff shows up in the history.

**Phase 2: Pick a project that uses several features**
The strongest options are the ones that combine features and show evidence:
- **#02 "Prove what Continuous Memory saves"** is the easiest to make rigorous. Run the same tasks with and without Graph and Brain. Measure tokens, time and correctness, and link the sessions behind each run. The numbers make a clear story.
- **#01 (handoff Claude Code → Codex)** makes the best live demo.
- **#09 (checkpoint-to-demo generator)** has the best output, because it produces a shareable page.

My pick is to build #02 on planworldsimulator itself. Use Brain for handoffs and Trails for review, and generate a #09-style report page as the deliverable. That one project touches checkpoints, Graph, Brain, Trails and a second agent.

**Phase 3: Polish for judges (last 2–3 hours)**
- Add a README with a clear problem statement, results and links to checkpoints and sessions.
- Make a 2–3 minute demo that shows the evidence, not just claims.
- Make sure everything is pushed and indexed before the deadline. Sync lag is up to an hour, so push early.
- Run `entire doctor` once more to check for stuck sessions or disconnected checkpoint branches.

**Risks**
- The org-admin import is the main blocker. Without it nothing shows up.
- Don't leave pushing to the last minute.

Want me to start on Phase 0 in this repo (checking for `entire`, running `entire enable`, setting up the plugins)? First, tell me whether this repo is under a GitHub org or your personal account, and if you know what the leaderboard scores.
Can you create a design-doc please and specify what additional setup steps are needed?
I'll check the repo and whether Entire is installed, so the doc reflects the actual state.

# PlanWorldSimulator world generator

Describe a planning benchmark in plain language and generate a playable world from it.
See [docs/design-decisions](docs/design-decisions) for the architecture.

The generator is a fake for now: it walks through the real steps (storyline, copy
template, fill template, tests) and writes a world folder, but does no LLM work.

## Layout

| Path                  | What it is                                                  |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/web`             | Website (Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind)                 |
| `src/backend`         | API (FastAPI, SQLite via SQLAlchemy and Alembic)            |
| `src/worlds-template` | Base template every world is copied from                    |
| `src/worlds`          | Generated worlds, one folder each (contents are gitignored) |

## Run it

```sh
just up      # build, start in the background, wait until healthy
just down    # stop (database and generated worlds are kept)
```

Open http://localhost:8480 (API docs on http://localhost:8400/docs). If another program uses
those ports, `just up` says so; set `PLANWORLDSIMULATOR_WEB_PORT` and
`PLANWORLDSIMULATOR_API_PORT` in `.env` to change them. Other commands: `just build`, `just logs [service]`,
`just ps`, `just reset` (also deletes the database volume) and `just dev` (live
reload, site on http://localhost:5173). Copy `.env.example` to `.env` to change
defaults.

## Develop

Needs [pixi](https://pixi.sh), [pnpm](https://pnpm.io) and [just](https://just.systems).

```sh
just install
just format
just lint
just typecheck
just test
```

What was chosen?

# Enable Entire to capture agent sessions as checkpoints

**Date:** 2026-10-10  
**Status:** proposed

## Context

Most of this repository is written by coding agents (Claude Code, Codex): the
Template Generator produces whole worlds, and the base template is built the
same way (see decision 0001). A commit shows what changed, but not the prompts,
reasoning and tool calls behind it. That context is lost once the session ends.

We want every agent-written commit to link back to the session that produced
it, so a change can be reviewed and understood later.

## Decision

Use [Entire](https://entire.io) to record agent sessions as checkpoints linked
to commits.

- **Agents covered:** Codex and Claude Code. Entire also generated hook files
  for Cursor (`.cursor/hooks.json`); these are committed with the rest, but
  Cursor is not a supported workflow.
- **Checkpoint storage:** `git-refs` (the default), so checkpoints travel with
  `git push` and no extra service is needed to store them.
- **Telemetry:** off (`--telemetry=false`).
- **Hooks:** `--absolute-git-hook-path`, so git hooks work regardless of the
  `PATH` in the shell or GUI that runs git.
- **Committed vs. local:**

  | Path | Committed | Why |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `.entire/settings.json`, `.entire/.gitignore` | yes | Shared project config. |
  | `.claude/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json`, `.cursor/hooks.json` | yes | Agent hooks that call `entire hooks ...`. Each hook exits quietly when `entire` is not installed, so contributors without it are not blocked. |
  | `.entire/logs/`, `metadata/`, `tmp/`, `settings.local.json` | no | Already ignored by `.entire/.gitignore`; local state. |

- **Per-person setup:** each contributor installs Entire and runs the setup in
  their own clone (see the implementation plan). Hooks are shared; the login
  and the git hook installation are not.
- **Server side:** the repository owner connects the repository through the
  Entire GitHub App. Without it, checkpoints are still pushed but sessions do
  not appear in Entire.

## Consequences

- Easier: reviewing agent-written commits with their full session context;
  explaining why a generated world or template looks the way it does.
- Required: every contributor runs the local setup once per clone; sessions
  started before setup are not captured, so start fresh sessions afterwards.
- Required: answer *yes* to the "link the commit to session context" prompt,
  or the commit has no checkpoint.
- Risk: session transcripts can contain secrets or private data, and
  checkpoints are pushed to the remote. Keep secrets out of prompts and review
  what Entire's redaction covers before making the repository public.
- Deferred: enforcing checkpoints in CI, and any non-`git-refs` storage.

## Alternatives considered

- **Do nothing; rely on commit messages and PR descriptions.** Cheap, but the
  reasoning and failed attempts are lost, which is the context we most want.
- **Commit session transcripts into the repository.** Pollutes history and
  diffs, and is hard to redact.
- **Use each agent's own local history.** Per machine and per tool, so it is
  not shared and does not link to commits.

## Implementation plan

1. **Install and sign in** (once per machine):

   ```sh
   curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
   entire login
   ```

2. **Enable in the clone** (already run once by the first contributor):

   ```sh
   entire enable --agent codex --telemetry=false --absolute-git-hook-path
   entire agent add claude-code
   entire agent list
   entire status
   ```

3. **Commit the shared config** (`.entire/settings.json`, `.entire/.gitignore`,
   `.claude/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json`, `.cursor/hooks.json`) in one
   change, after reviewing each file for local-only content.
4. **Verify a checkpoint:** start fresh Codex and Claude Code sessions, make a
   small change, commit it (answer *yes* to linking), then:

   ```sh
   entire checkpoint list
   entire checkpoint explain HEAD
   ```

5. **Push and connect:** push the commit; the repository owner installs the
   Entire GitHub App for this repository.
6. **Document it:** add a short "Contributing with agents" note to the README
   pointing at this decision.

Acceptance criteria:

- `entire status` reports enabled with `git-refs` storage and telemetry off.
- A commit made from a fresh Claude Code session and one from a fresh Codex
  session each show a checkpoint in `entire checkpoint list`.
- After the push, both sessions appear in Entire for the connected repository.
- A clone without `entire` installed can still run Claude Code and Codex
  without hook errors.

## Supersedes

None.

# Use Continuous Memory for the Entire hackathon

**Date:** 2026-10-10  
**Status:** proposed

## Context

We are competing at Agentic AI Hack Zürich 2026 in the Entire track and want to
rank as high as possible. The brief does not say how the leaderboard is scored,
so we assume two things count: how deeply the Entire features are used (real
checkpoints, Trails, Graph, Brain), and how convincing the project is, with
evidence behind its claims.

Decision 0002 already enables checkpoints. This repository is a good test bed:
agents generate whole worlds (decision 0001), and generation runs are long,
repeatable and measurable.

## Decision

Build the brief's idea **"Prove what Continuous Memory saves"** (#02) on this
repository, and make the work itself a showcase of the Entire features.

- **Experiment:** run the same set of world-generation and coding tasks in two
  arms, *baseline* (no Graph, no Brain) and *continuous memory* (Graph and Brain
  active). Per run, record tokens (`entire graph stats --repo .`), wall time,
  and correctness (the world's tests pass, plus a rubric check).
- **Tasks:** 4 to 6 fixed prompts of mixed type: add an API route, change the
  template, fix a seeded bug, extend an existing world. Each runs in a fresh
  session, with at least two runs per arm to show variance.
- **Handoff (brief idea #01):** one task starts in Claude Code and finishes in
  Codex. Brain carries the decisions across, with no re-briefing.
- **Review:** all changes go through Trails with the default Runners, so every
  push is evaluated and linked to a PR.
- **Deliverable:** a results page (brief idea #09), generated from checkpoints,
  with a table per task and links to the session behind every number.
- **Rule:** every commit is made from a captured session and linked to its
  checkpoint (answer *yes* to the prompt).

## Consequences

- Easier: a clear story with numbers; all four core features are used for real;
  every claim links to a session.
- Required: the experiment must be fair. Same model, same prompts, clean
  sessions, and the arms are not mixed in one session.
- Risk: results may show little or no saving on a small repository. We report
  what we measure; a negative or mixed result with honest evidence is still a
  valid outcome.
- Risk: Trails needs a feature flag, and repository import needs an org admin.
  Both can delay us (see setup).
- Deferred: building a new agent integration, and the other brief ideas.

## Alternatives considered

# Create Commits

Create one or more focused commits from the changes in the working tree. Use
this skill when the user asks to commit their work; do not use it merely to
draft a commit message. This skill commits locally only — it never pushes or
opens a pull request.

## Inspect before committing

1. Inspect the current branch, worktree, staged and unstaged changes, and
   recent commits for style and scope conventions.
2. Require changes to commit. If the worktree is already clean, report that and
   stop.
3. Do not create a branch, push, rewrite history, or amend existing commits
   unless the user explicitly requests it.
4. Group the changes into focused commits, each covering one logical change.
   Prefer several small commits over one mixed commit. Confirm the grouping with
   the user when a single set of changes spans unrelated concerns.

## Create the commit(s)

1. Stage only the files that belong to each commit. Do not stage unrelated
   changes, build artifacts, or secrets.
2. Use a Conventional Commit-style subject:

   ```text
   <type>(<optional-scope>): <imperative summary>
   ```

   Use `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `docs`, `test`, `chore`, `ci`, `build`,
   `perf`, or `revert`. Omit the scope when it does not make the subject
   clearer. Keep the subject in the imperative mood and roughly under 72
   characters.
3. Draft the body from [the commit-message template](references/commit-message-template.md).
   Remove unused bullets. Add a `Notes` section only for a review-relevant
   limitation, migration, decision, or follow-up. Omit the body entirely for a
   trivial change whose subject is self-explanatory.
4. Create each commit, for example:

   ```sh
   git commit -F <message-file>
   ```

   Use a message file rather than repeated `-m` flags so the body keeps its
   structure.
5. Return a summary of the commits created (subject and scope of each) and the
   verification performed.

## Identity and attribution

Git attributes the commit to the configured user. Do not set or alter Git
author or committer identity. Never add a `Co-authored-by` trailer to a commit.
Likewise, never add `Assisted-by`, AI attribution, or any equivalent
attribution to commit messages.
